title: The Case for Free Choice
objective: After this level you can explain libertarian free will, the view that some choices are not fixed by prior causes, and why its defenders find it necessary for blame and praise.
summary: Libertarians hold that some choices aren’t fixed by prior causes, since blame needs alternatives; agent-causal views make the agent the cause, and critics raise luck.

cards.headline: Think of a choice you regret.
cards.body: When you kick yourself over it, you’re assuming something big: that you could have chosen and done otherwise. One camp of philosophers says that assumption is exactly right.

cards.headline: A real fork in the road
cards.body: Libertarians about free will hold that we do have free will, and that a free choice must not be causally determined by factors beyond your control. Right up to the moment you decide, more than one road is truly open. Most libertarians add that this freedom to do otherwise is needed for moral responsibility. So if determinism were true, they say, free will would be gone.

cards.headline: Why blame needs it
cards.body: Think about how excuses work. If a bully forced someone to steal a classmate’s lunch, blaming the thief no longer seems fair: the alternatives were gone. Libertarians push the point all the way. We act freely and are responsible, the slogan goes, only if we are the ultimate source of our actions. A domino is never the ultimate source of anything.

cards.headline: A prime mover unmoved
cards.body: How could you be the source? Agent-causal libertarians, from Thomas Reid in 1788 to Roderick Chisholm, say the agent herself causes a free choice, not just her prior beliefs and desires. Chisholm put it boldly in 1964: “Each of us, when we act, is a prime mover unmoved.” You cause things to happen, and nothing causes you to cause them.

cards.headline: Freedom, or just luck?
cards.body: Critics answer with the luck objection. If nothing before your choice settles which way it goes, then the difference between choosing one way and the other looks like chance, nature’s roll of the dice. That seems no better for blame than determinism. Robert Kane replies that if you make an effort to do what you believe you ought, and succeed, the choice is still yours.

cards.headline: The Case for Free Choice: the big picture
learned: Libertarians: some choices aren’t fixed by prior causes
Blame seems to need real alternatives
Chisholm: each of us is a prime mover unmoved
Critics: an unfixed choice looks like luck

questions.prompt: According to libertarians about free will, what must be true of a free choice?

options.label: It is fixed by prior causes but still feels open to you
It is decided by the laws of nature and nothing else
options.rationale: They deny free choices are fixed that way.

options.label: It is not causally determined by factors beyond your control
It is chosen for you by the community you belong to
options.rationale: Libertarians put the source in the agent.

questions.explanation: Libertarians hold that a free choice must not be causally determined by factors beyond the agent’s control.

questions.prompt: Why do libertarians think blame needs choices that aren’t fixed in advance?

options.label: Because blame only deters people who could act otherwise
options.rationale: Their reason is fairness, not deterrence.

options.label: Because blaming seems unfair when someone had no alternative
Because regret always proves a choice was free
options.rationale: Regret shows the assumption; it proves nothing.

options.label: Because Laplace showed choices can’t be predicted

questions.explanation: Once someone’s alternatives are gone, as with the coerced lunch thief, blame no longer seems fair; libertarians say responsibility needs us to be the ultimate source of what we do.

questions.prompt: Level 5 called where a change comes from its efficient cause. On the agent-causal view, what is the efficient cause of a free choice?

options.label: The state of the world long before
Pure chance with no cause at all
options.rationale: The agent causes it; it isn’t uncaused.

questions.explanation: Agent-causal libertarians say the agent causes the choice: in Chisholm’s words, each of us is a prime mover unmoved.
